title: SLO-driven token-bucket queueing and throttler (design draft)
content:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a pragmatic, SLO-driven per-tenant admission and queueing system based on token-buckets + priority queues. Goal is to bound p95/p99 latency regressions while maximizing throughput on common-case cache hits and preserving predictable costs for tenants.

Context / motivation:
- Existing cluster-level admission is all-or-nothing and does not respect tenant SLOs or cache hit patterns.
- We need predictable tail latency even under sudden load spikes (thundering herd, noisy neighbors).
- Kernels and batching layers are most efficient when they can form reasonably full batches, but waiting too long hurts latency SLOs.

High-level approach (summary):
1) Per-tenant token-bucket rate limit that expresses the steady-state throughput guarantee derived from tenant SLOs and their committed capacity or observed behavior.
2) Small, prioritized in-memory queues per tenant (short -> medium -> low priority). Each request is mapped to a priority based on request attributes (SLO class, enterprise override, cache hit hint).
3) A shared burst pool to allow short spikes beyond per-tenant steady rate, reclaimed over time.
4) Admission decision: accept-execute / enqueue-with-timeout / reject (429). Enqueue timeouts are computed from SLO budget and current token deficit.
5) Cache-awareness: KV-cache hits consume fewer or zero tokens and are eligible for a fast-path queue that is polled with shorter wait thresholds.
6) Kernel hinting: scheduler attaches expected token-cost & priority to requests so worker schedulers can assemble batches that respect latency budgets and token accounting.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not propose a full RBAC/contract billing hook; pricing integration is a follow-up.
- Not covering on-prem single-tenant optimizations (they can opt out).

Key concepts and definitions:
- Token unit: normalized request weight. Base token cost = 1 for a small text-generation call with short prompt. Token cost scales with expected output token count x compute-intensity factor (model family + quantization).
- Refill interval: a sliding-window token refill computed per-tenant; default 1s but tunable to align with kernel batching cadence.
- Burst pool: cluster-level borrowable tokens with a rate limiter to avoid exhaustion. Tenants borrowing from the pool are deprioritized for refill until borrow penalty decays.
- Fast-path queue: micro-queue polled at higher frequency for cache-hit or low-compute requests. Designed to keep cache benefits from being negated by queueing delays.

How to derive per-tenant rates from SLOs:
- Given tenant p95 latency SLO and average model latency (from perf profiles), estimate tokens/sec needed to meet p95 at baseline concurrency.
- For committed dedicated tenants: use contract throughput as baseline. For free-tier/self-serve: use recent 5m sustained throughput clipped by configured caps.
- Example: Tenant A p95 target 350ms, average model latency 90ms => target concurrency ~ p95/avg ~= 3.9 => tokens/sec ~= concurrency / avg_latency_seconds -> translate to tokens/sec. (Appendix will show conversion math and examples.)

Queue structure and prioritization:
- Each tenant has 3 queues: urgent, normal, background.
- Assignment rules (examples):
  - urgent: admin API calls, enterprise SLO-critical routes, system health pings
  - normal: typical generation/chat requests
  - background: batch embeddings, low-priority async jobs
- Queue sizes: small fixed in-memory ring buffers (configurable per-tenant) to avoid head-of-line blocking across tenants. Overflow policy: tail-drop + early-reject for background; normal/urgent attempt borrow from burst pool before rejecting.

Admission algorithm (per incoming request):
1) Compute estimated token_cost based on model_id, seq_len_estimate, and cached compute profile (lookup).
2) Check per-tenant tokens available. If enough, accept and deduct tokens immediately.
3) If not enough, check fast-path eligibility: if cache_hit_hint==true and fast-path queue has capacity -> enqueue to fast-path with tight timeout (e.g., 30-80ms).
4) Otherwise, try normal enqueue with timeout computed from token deficit and SLO slack. If expected wait > max_wait_for_route -> reject with 429 and include retry-after header.
5) Refill tokens on sliding-window schedule; when tokens become available, dequeuer picks highest-priority tenant+queue that still fits into batch latency budgets.

Timeout policy and client-visible errors:
- Timeout tiers:
  - fast-path: 30-80ms (for cache hits / tiny outputs)
  - normal: configurable per-tenant based on SLO slack (default p95_target/3)
  - background: up to several seconds or background-specific prefs
- If a request times out in queue, return 429 (retryable) with a structured body pointing to quota details. For requests nearing timeout while in worker dispatch, prefer graceful degrade (model fallback) rather than immediate abort if configured.

KV-cache integration:
- Cache-hit hinting: front-end proxy can include a cache_hit_hint boolean based on prefix match / quick local pre-check; true hits go to fast-path.
- Token reduction: actual cache hit observed at execution time triggers a partial refund (e.g., reimburse 70-100% of tokens) to the tenant token pool and increments cache-win metrics. This encourages cache-friendly traffic and corrects overcharge for optimistic cost estimates.
- Cache-warm prefetching: when enqueuing a likely hot prefix, we may schedule a low-priority prefill that consumes tokens from a special prefill budget, not the regular token budget.

Kernel scheduling hints and batching:
- Each queued request carries metadata: token_cost_estimate, priority, enqueue_deadline_ms.
- Worker-side batcher will group requests maximizing expected batch size while respecting earliest enqueue_deadline among grouped requests (i.e., wait until oldest deadline - guard to avoid undue tail latency).
- Batch composition policy: prefer homogeneous model families & quantization levels for kernel efficiency. If mixing, prefer smallest common denominator kernels or split batches.
- If a batch is formed with requests from multiple tenants, token deduction is performed atomically per-tenant at dispatch time; if a tenant’s tokens were consumed by other dispatches meanwhile, dispatch may evict that tenant’s requests from batch and either replace or execute smaller batch. Evictions should be rare and penalized in metrics.

Fairness and multi-tenant behaviors:
- Deficit-based fairness: tenants have long-term deficit counters to ensure heavy hitters don't starve small tenants over extended periods.
- Emergency fallback: cluster-level admission can flip to strict mode under sustained overload, enforcing hard per-tenant caps and disabling burst pool. Alerting and an automated circuit-breaker will be triggered.

Observability and metrics (minimum set):
- per_tenant_tokens_available (gauge)
- per_tenant_queue_length{priority}
- per_tenant_enqueue_latency_histogram
- cluster_burst_pool_usage (gauge)
- token_refill_rate_per_tenant (counter)
- queue_timeouts_by_tenant (counter)
- cache_hit_token_refunds (counter)
- kernel_batch_size_distribution
- dispatch_evictions (counter) + eviction_reasons (labels)
- SLA_breach_incidents (log / alert)

Tracing and dashboards:
- Trace spans: frontend -> admission -> enqueue -> dequeuer -> batch-> kernel -> response. Include token_charge and token_refund annotations.
- Dashboards: tenant SLO heatmap (p50/p95/p99), queue depth & timeout rate, burst pool trends, kernel batch efficiency vs latency.

Failure modes and mitigation:
- Incorrect token cost estimates: mitigation via conservative over-estimate and refunds on cache hit + continuous learning of per-route cost models.
- Starvation of low-priority tenants: enforce minimal guaranteed tokens for all paying tiers; accelerated refill for starving tenants underutilizing capacity.
- Cache incorrectness (front-end hint false positive): refunds handled at execution time. Maintain a small penalty to front-end if hints are wildly inaccurate.

Operational considerations and rollout plan:
1) Implement token accounting primitives and local-only queues; unit tests + simulation harness (see JIRA-INF-5421).
2) Canary: enable in one region, 5% of traffic, surface metrics. Run for 2 weeks, tune defaults.
3) Gradual ramp to 25% then 100% for self-serve clusters; enterprise/dedicated customers may opt-in earlier.
4) Post-rollout: enable automated parameter tuning process (lightweight ML) to adjust refill rates based on observed utilization and SLO breach signals.

Compatibility and config knobs:
- Tenants can set override knobs: min_tokens, max_burst, background_queue_enabled, enterprise_priority_flag.
- Dedicated clusters can disable the burst pool and use static caps.

Appendix A: example parameter table (toy)
- Tenant X: p95_target=350ms, avg_latency=110ms, derived_tokens_per_sec=3, burst=6, fastpath_enabled=true
- Tenant Y (free): cap_tokens_per_sec=1, burst=2, fastpath_enabled=false

Appendix B: open questions / research items
- Best conversion function from SLO targets to tokens/sec for multi-model tenants (mix of small+large models).
- Whether to allow token trading between related tenants (org-level pooling).
- How aggressive should refund policy be for cache hits vs potential abuse?
- Feasibility of ML-based admission predictor that learns immediate acceptance probability and replaces static token estimate.

References and related work:
- Prior notes: Scheduler backpressure draft (internal), tenant-aware queueing notes (internal).
- External: literature on token-bucket ingress, deficit round robin, and deadline-aware batching.

Next steps / action items:
- Prototype token accounting library (owner: Diego) - JIRA-INF-5421
- Integrate fast-path KV hints into front-end proxy (owner: Sara) - PR link in linked_artifacts
- Simulation harness to stress test fairness and eviction behavior (owner: Tom)
- Ops dashboard template and alerts (owner: Priya)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally prescriptive but conservative — prefer safety and predictable SLO behavior over aggressive throughput wins in the first iteration. Feedback requested on: token unit definition, refund ratios for cache hits, and sensible defaults for fast-path timeouts.

End of draft.
